text: Role-based access control, least privilege, segregation of duties, access reviews, privileged access — this chapter covers five real controls. Access governance is the program that coordinates all five: who decides, who grants, who checks.

Access governance answers four questions for every system worth protecting. Who can request access? Who has the authority to approve it? Who actually grants it? And who checks, afterward, that the grant was correct and is still needed?

Most access changes trace back to three events. Joiner — a new hire gets starting access tied to their role. Mover — someone changes teams and needs new access, and critically, needs their old access removed. Leaver — someone exits, and every grant they held gets revoked, fast.

Every access decision involves four roles. The requester identifies the need. The approver — usually the data owner — decides if it's justified. The provisioner executes the grant. The auditor confirms, independently, that it was approved and is still appropriate.

Next up: role-based access control — the single most common way organizations actually implement the access governance program this lesson described, mapping people to roles instead of granting permissions one person at a time.
